title: Yara and the Radiators
premise: After her mother's funeral, Rosalind Joubert returns to the family house to catalog a lifetime of unspoken things — most of all, what happened the summer her father disappeared and the family quietly rearranged itself around the silence. When Amara Diallo, the last fluent speaker of a dying neighborhood language, asks Rosalind to become her final student, the lessons begin to unlock words Rosalind was never taught to say. As the old district faces demolition and the last bus route is rerouted, Rosalind discovers that her aunt, the family's benevolent matriarch, engineered both the silence and the erasure of the language that could have exposed it. In the end, Rosalind must choose between protecting the found family that raised her and speaking the truth aloud in Amara's tongue at the final community gathering — a choice that costs her the inheritance but gives her back her voice.
about_author: Astrid Almeida is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloging private letters and unfinished manuscripts in coastal cities. Their fiction explores inheritance, silence, and the languages families invent to avoid the truth.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Almost
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Three days after the funeral, she begins cataloging her mother's house room by room, finding drawers of unlabeled keys and letters never sent. The emotional beat is grief sharpened into avoidance: every object points toward the summer of 1998, which no relative will name.

chapters.title: Aunt Odile's Ledger
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At the wake, Aunt Odile presides with warm authority, distributing tasks and closing conversations like doors. She hands Rosalind a ledger of family debts and favors, saying some pages are 'not for reading.' Rosalind obeys, and hates herself for it.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Speaks Alone
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Delivering donated furniture to the old neighborhood, Rosalind meets Amara Diallo, an elderly woman who talks to herself in Kavungu, a language only she still speaks. Amara mistakes her for someone else — 'the Joubert girl who listens' — and Rosalind doesn't correct her.

chapters.title: One Final Student
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Amara reflects on outliving everyone who shared her tongue and decides Rosalind will be her last student, whether the girl knows it or not. She leaves a note in Kavungu on Rosalind's windshield. The beat is fierce, unsentimental hope.

chapters.title: First Words
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Against her better judgment, Rosalind takes the bus to the old district for a first lesson. Amara teaches her greetings, then one forbidden word: 'mbengi' — the thing hidden under the floor. Rosalind feels the word land in her body like a bruise.

chapters.title: What the Family Arranged
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile learns Rosalind has been visiting the old neighborhood and quietly intervenes: a job offer, a rent subsidy, gentle pressure to move across town. Her chapter reveals she loves her family fiercely and controls them completely, and cannot tell the difference anymore.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The city announces the 47 bus line — the last route into the old district — will be rerouted in four months for redevelopment. Rosalind realizes Amara's world has an expiration date, and so does her access to the truth.

chapters.title: Lessons in the Blue Kitchen
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Weekly lessons deepen; Amara teaches through cooking, songs, and proverbs, each one accidentally brushing against 1998. Rosalind learns the phrase 'the child who carried the letter,' and recognizes herself. She goes home shaken and says nothing at dinner.

chapters.title: Cousin Theo Breaks Rank
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, Odile's son and Rosalind's childhood ally, admits he's been skimming from the family accounts to fund his own escape. He begs Rosalind for silence, making her complicit — and showing her how easily loyalty becomes a leash.

chapters.title: The Letter Under the Floor
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Following Amara's proverb about floors, Rosalind pries up a board in her mother's closet and finds her father's last letter, written in Kavungu, addressed to her. She can't read it. She hides it inside Odile's ledger, unread.

chapters.title: Translation as Betrayal
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Amara recognizes the sealed letter's shape when Rosalind describes it and realizes whose daughter this is. She offers to translate it, then withdraws, fearing she'll destroy the girl's family. The beat is the cruelty of kindness withheld.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Architect
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Odile hosts the developer behind the rerouting, and Rosalind watches her aunt charm the demolition of the neighborhood over dessert. Rosalind almost speaks, almost asks, and instead passes the salt. Shame curdles into resolve.

chapters.title: Mbengi
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind confronts Amara: translate the letter or teach me enough to read it myself. Amara chooses the second, and over three brutal weeks Rosalind works through her father's handwriting. The letter reveals he discovered Odile had falsified the deed that displaced forty families — including Amara's — and that he died fleeing to expose it.

chapters.title: The Weight of Knowing
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo discovers Rosalind has the letter and panics; exposure would ruin him too. He gives her an ultimatum wrapped in love: burn it, or lose him. Rosalind spends a sleepless night holding both truths — the family that raised her, the truth that defines her.

chapters.title: Odile's Version
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Sensing the walls closing in, Odile tells Rosalind her own story: how she took the deed to save the family from ruin, how Rosalind's mother begged her to bury it, how silence was the price of keeping everyone fed. It is half true, and entirely self-forgiving.

chapters.title: The Last Bus
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. The 47 runs its final route into the old district. Rosalind rides it end to end with Amara, past shuttered shops and the lot where her father's evidence once lived. Amara tells her: 'A language dies when its speakers decide the truth costs too much.'

chapters.title: The Gathering
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Amara hosts a final community gathering to mark the language's end, and asks Rosalind to speak. With Odile, Theo, and the whole arranged family in the audience, Rosalind stands, opens her father's letter, and reads it aloud — first in Kavungu, then in English.

chapters.title: Aftermath in the Blue Kitchen
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The family fractures: Theo flees, cousins take sides, Odile sits alone in the kitchen where she once ruled. For the first time she speaks without managing anyone, admitting what she did — not to be forgiven, but because silence finally costs more than truth.

chapters.title: What Remains of the House
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. Rosalind signs away her inheritance, funding legal aid for the displaced families and a Kavungu archive in Amara's name. She keeps only the ledger's blank pages and her father's letter. The beat is grief that has finally become usable.

chapters.title: Student and Teacher
chapters.summary: Amara's POV. Amara, unexpectedly, does not die with her language: recordings, a small class of children, and one fluent student. She assesses Rosalind's accent with tyrannical delight and declares, grudgingly, that the tongue will outlive her after all.

chapters.title: The Question
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV. At her mother's grave, Rosalind finally asks the question the whole family arranged itself around — aloud, to the stone, in two languages. There is no answer, and for the first time that feels like enough. She boards the new bus line, going forward instead of back.

chapters.title: Yara
chapters.summary: Rosalind's POV, coda. A year later, Rosalind teaches a Saturday class in the old district's community hall, where a girl named Yara asks what 'mbengi' means. Rosalind answers honestly: the thing hidden under the floor, and the courage to lift the board. The language, like the truth, now belongs to whoever carries it.
